questions.q: What should you check before running terraform apply to provision six Standard_NC24ads_A100_v4 VMs?
options: That the region's GPU family quota can actually support six VMs of that size
Nothing -- Terraform automatically requests quota increases on your behalf
That the VMs are tagged with a cost center
That Kubernetes is already running a device plugin
questions.explain: GPU quota is checked before writing Terraform at all -- a fleet of six GPU VMs that exceeds the region's quota fails apply partway through, not cleanly up front.

questions.q: In this lab's Terraform config, what does the custom_data bootstrap script do on each GPU VM?
options: Only installs a monitoring agent
Only joins the VM to the Kubernetes cluster, with no driver setup
Nothing -- custom_data is unused by azurerm_linux_virtual_machine
Installs the NVIDIA driver and Container Toolkit, then runs the kubeadm join command, so the node is both driver-ready and a cluster member when it finishes booting
questions.explain: Running both steps in the same bootstrap script means a node only finishes booting once it's genuinely ready for GPU workloads and already part of the cluster.

questions.q: Why does the lab apply both a node label (accelerator=nvidia-a100) and a taint (nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule) to the GPU nodes?
options: The taint alone is sufficient and the label is only cosmetic
The label is required only for billing reports
The label pulls GPU-requesting pods onto the nodes via nodeSelector, while the taint keeps ordinary pods from landing there by accident -- both are needed together
Labels and taints do the exact same thing, so either one works alone
questions.explain: A selector alone pulls the right pods in; a taint is what actively keeps the wrong ones out. The pairing is what makes GPU nodes safe to share a cluster with everything else.

questions.q: If kubectl describe node shows nvidia.com/gpu: 0 on a newly joined node, what does this lab say to check first?
options: Re-run terraform apply from scratch
The device plugin pod's logs on that specific node -- it likely didn't start cleanly
The VM's admin_username setting
The Azure subscription's billing status
questions.explain: A node reporting zero GPU capacity almost always means its device plugin pod failed to start correctly, not that the hardware or driver is missing.

questions.q: What is the actual end-to-end proof this lab is built around?
options: terraform apply completing with no errors
nvidia-smi printing a GPU table on one single VM
The device plugin DaemonSet showing as deployed in kubectl get pods
A real training Job (defect-model-training-run-42) scheduling onto a GPU node and reaching the Running state, not just each setup step succeeding in isolation
questions.explain: Each individual step succeeding doesn't guarantee the whole chain works -- only a real workload actually scheduling and running on a real GPU proves quota, Terraform, drivers, and scheduling all line up.
